NATURE CLUB LESSON · NATURE CLUB ANIMALS · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Coastal Animals — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the shore crew and its easiest ID trick, one wave at a time.

What is this?

Coastal animals live at the meeting line of land and sea: the seal, the sea lion, the pelican and the puffin — half their life on rocks, half in the waves.

What does it mean?

Two worlds, one animal: the shore crew breathes air, raises babies on land, and hunts in the sea — the beach is their doorstep.

What does the child need to know?

Sea lions have little ear flaps and can walk on all four flippers; true seals have no ear flaps and scoot on their bellies; pelican pouches stretch to hold several liters of fish-and-water; puffins fly underwater with their wings and carry fish crosswise in their beaks.

Why this matters

Beach days are seal-and-pelican days in much of the US, UK and Canada — the card turns every coastal walk into a who&rsquo;s-who.

What it teaches

Observation and ID by detail (ear flaps!), body-movement imitation, and beach ethics: watch from a distance, never chase a resting seal.

Words to learn

coastsealsea lionear flapspelicanpouchpuffincolonyrockstide

Say this to your child

“"Coastal animals live on the beach&rsquo;s doorstep! The seal slides, the sea lion walks and barks, the pelican scoops fish in its pouch, and the puffin flies underwater. How to tell the seal cousins: look for the ear flaps!"”

Step by step

  1. The seal: the belly-slider — no ear flaps, and on land it wriggles like a caterpillar; in water it is a torpedo.
  2. The sea lion: the walker — ear flaps and rotating back flippers let it "walk"; it barks like a dog and claps on cue.
  3. The pelican: the pouch — scoop, drain, swallow: the pouch is a net and a lunchbox. Pelicans fly in lines and glide low over the waves.
  4. The puffin: the underwater parrot — wings do both jobs, and the beak carries a whole row of fish crosswise for the chick.
  5. The shore rule: a sleeping seal is off-duty — give it room, keep dogs leashed, and report stranded pups to a ranger.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the seal lies smooth and earless, the sea lion props up on its flippers, the pelican shows the famous pouch, and the puffin wears its rainbow beak. Spot the ear flaps — that is the tell.

Ask your child

"How do you tell a seal from a sea lion?" (ear flaps — sea lions have them) "What does the pelican use its pouch for?" (scooping fish like a net) "How does the puffin fly underwater?" (with its wings)

What your child can say or do

Your child might wriggle across every rug "seal-style", bark-and-clap like a sea lion on request, or pouch-scoop toys from the bath announcing "pelican!"

Out in the real world

Seal colonies haul out on coasts on both sides of the Atlantic — boardwalks and ranger stations mark the viewing spots. Puffin islands in the UK and Maine welcome boat trips in summer.

Try it together

Beach moves: seal wriggle on a rug, sea lion walk-and-bark, pelican scoop from the blue-carpet sea, puffin flap-splash. Finish with the ID quiz: ear flaps or no ear flaps?

Understanding check

Ask: "Which one has ear flaps?" (the sea lion) "How does the seal move on land?" (wriggling on its belly) "How many fish can a puffin carry at once?" (a whole row, crosswise)

This lesson pairs with the Coastal Animals flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Nature Club Animals.
